title: Plate Boundaries & Hazards
meta_desc: A-Level Geography adventure on plate boundaries, tectonic processes and Pacific Ring.
final_note: Most tectonic hazards concentrate on plate boundaries.

walkthroughs.body_html: Destructive plate margins host 90 percent of largest earthquakes (Mw > 8.5). At constructive boundaries, basaltic magma rises producing mild eruptions. Conservative margins (San Andreas) only generate earthquakes. Hotspots are intraplate (e.g. Hawaii, Yellowstone supervolcano).

75 percent of world's active volcanoes lie around Pacific; includes Japan, Indonesia, Philippines, Alaska, Cascadia, Andes. 90 percent of global earthquakes. Subduction zones produce explosive andesitic-dacitic eruptions. Mount Pinatubo 1991 (VEI 6) cooled global climate 0.5 degrees C.

Hawaii: Pacific Plate moves NW at 7 cm/yr over stationary mantle plume. Loihi seamount forming next island. Yellowstone supervolcano caldera (Wyoming); last major eruption Lava Creek 640 ka VEI 8 ejected 1000 km^3 ash. Iceland sits on both ridge and hotspot.

mcqs.q: Why are there no volcanoes at conservative plate boundaries?
options: There are volcanoes at conservative boundaries — that's where most of them form.
Plates move because of ocean tides pulling on the crust.
There are no volcanoes because the boundaries are too cold.
Conservative boundaries involve plates sliding past each other horizontally — no crust is created or destroyed, so there is no subduction to generate magma.

mcqs.q: What drives the movement of tectonic plates?
options: There are volcanoes at conservative boundaries — that's where most of them form.
The Earth's rotation makes the plates move.
Plates move because of ocean tides pulling on the crust.
Convection currents in the mantle combined with slab pull at subduction zones and ridge push at constructive boundaries.

mcqs.q: What happens at a constructive (divergent) plate boundary?
options: Plates move because of ocean tides pulling on the crust.
At constructive boundaries the plates collide and build mountains.
Plates move apart, magma rises to fill the gap and solidifies, forming new oceanic crust — for example at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
At constructive boundaries the plates slide past each other sideways.
